As Harold Meyerson writes this week in *The Washington Post* in the article, *How to ease economic anxiety*, that the general consensus is that America is downwardly mobile and doesn't know what it can do to arrest, much less reverse, this trend. In a recent survey 49% of the respondents said they felt that only the upper class could realistically expect to be able to pay for their children's college education. Another 46 percent said that only the upper class should expect to be able to save enough to retire comfortably. Fully 59 percent said they were concerned about falling out of their current economic class over the next few years. This survey suggests that the public is aware of this downward trend. Since the end of World War II the expectations of economic security and mobility that were widely shared by Americans and this has been replaced by a pervasive economic anxiety. The problem is that anxiety won't change things. As Meyerson writes, *neither will the majority of analyses of how we got into this fix, nor will most of the (relatively few) solutions that are being proposed.* The problem is that when people find themselves in a situation where they feel that neither party like former private equity banker and Obama administration official Steven Rattner, writing in the *New York Times*, *the lack of wage growth owes much to the continuing effects of globalization, a trend that has benefited the United States as a whole while hurting many workers.* Good for America, apparently, but bad for Americans. Besides, he implies, who can do anything about globalization? It's as inexorable as the sunrise. Most American workers, however, are not in competition with their counterparts in Mexico and China - not if they work at Wal-Mart or drive a truck. The downward pressure that globalization exerts on wages spills over to other sectors, but it's not more than a secondary cause for pervasive income stagnation. The primary cause is that, with collective bargaining nearly dead (just 6.6 percent of private-sector workers belong to unions), there is no pressure on employers to share their productivity gains with their workers. And with the rise of shareholder capitalism, there's considerable pressure to boost payouts to stockholders. The age of shareholder capitalism, most notably proclaimed by General Electric CEO Jack Welch in the early years of the Reagan presidency (while Welch was famously off-shoring much of GE's manufacturing), has, like the age of globalization, also coincided with the age of wage stagnation. But moving from a shareholder capitalism that has diminished most Americans' share of the national pie to a stakeholder capitalism that distributes a greater share of company revenue to the workers who produce it will require major changes to our political economy. It will require the remaining unions to organize millions of workers whom they don't enroll as members now, who can nonetheless agitate for better pay and conditions. It will require the labor movement to build a strong political council to set the kind of wage standards - and not just minimum-wage standards - that workers once were able to win for themselves before the advent of shareholder capitalism. It will require the rebirth of the kind of economic left in the United States that gave us the New Deal and the four ensuing decades of broadly shared prosperity. I'll order less, but the alternative is just more anxiety, and all its attendant pathologies.

If you asked the average American they will tell you that government is bloated and job growth has been anemic under the Obama Administration. After entering office the worst recession since the Great Depression and last month the economy added 165,000 jobs, and since President Obama took office the economy has added almost 2.5 million jobs, and almost all in the private sector. Dear Jeffrey, and Jeffrey: how sweet this note!
Hello Jeffrey, I'm very happy to meet you, whoever you may be. I somehow completely trust your fairy instincts.

Dear Jeffrey,
I would like to introduce you to my dear friend Jeffrey.
He is a very good friend of Lisa and Larry Summers. He previously brought Brian Boyd to Harvard and has a large group of scientists, and academics at his home. I truly think you would enjoy each others company.
Love,

I am often asked to give my views and to rate the distinguished list of today's various financiers. I hesitate to so my area of expertise is now philanthropy and was formerly technology. Money is a product of my past endeavors and the leverage to do so as my area of expertise is now philanthropy and was formerly technology. Money is a product of my past endeavors and the leverage for my future social goals. That being said, I would do so with the simple caveat that I am not an expert in this area. I have known Jeffrey Epstein for 15 years. I have never witnessed or heard of any inappropriate behavior. To the contrary, I have found him to be an engaging conversationalist, a devoted friend, and a philanthropist extraordinair. His interests are far and wide and unlike many that simply repeat back what they have read, he is creative and original in fields such as signal intelligence, power law distributions, and encryption. Different well what in his past he has made some awful decisions, and I'm sure like most of us, he has regrets. But I believe he has learned from those mistakes and has continued his charitable work what he began even decades before his legal issues. I have had the privilege to meet the world's greatest minds, and I can easily say that Jeffrey is amongst the best of those. I have utmost confidence in his integrity. I have dealt with him for number of years on both sides of a negotiation and say with certainty I'd rather be on his side. He has been in the Billionaire business for longer than almost anyone else. His insight into the unique problems of the super wealthy, has been invaluable to many others that I know. He found a niche in the early 80s discerning the burdens of hyper wealth and from his time on the board of Rockefeller or his time at the trilateral commission, his common refrain from those he has come in contact with Jeffrey has made me think differently about ___. He has an extraordinary ability with numbers, complex concepts, mixed with sometimes brutal honesty, refreshing, a sense of humor that some find highly cultured others find just outright hilary. His homes are probably the best collection of real estate in the united states. A private island, homes that some describe as a tribute to megalomania, and a ranch in new mexico that is truly beyond imagination and my favorite townhouse in NY. His attention to detail is remarkable. I find it sad that he doesn't have children of his own, but make up for it by maintaining close friendships that have lasted for decades. His charitable instincts have been honed over many years and his advice and judgment has been invaluable in several instances. His ability to explain complex derivatives or concepts on the bleeding edge of science in layman's terms is part of his teaching veneer. I have met many people who criticize those who maintain a friendship with Jeffrey, and group those opinions are impervious to change. However, in the vast majority of cases, it is with those that have never had the opportunity to sit with him for a lengthy period of time and understand the complexity of the issues he faces. I find it difficult to transition to another seemingly unrelated, only at the end to have the thread pulled tightly and ending with an elegant coda. I can call him and ask, can you explain this to me, and with an impish respond, and a breath of fresh air, if he can't, he simply says I don't know.

Maybe I can be in ny Thursday. Are you?

understood. i think the samsung opportunity , needs to be tweaked and taken. it would serve multiple purposes. (speak to me ) i don't believe you will be happy at samsung or at andresson. but samsung is more of a university, and andresson a small albeit interesting tech school. your skill set is not about investing . you can surely develop it, but it is really a 5 to 6 year curve. down the proverbial 20 or 10. It is narrow, and a very crowded space. you could advise andresson while still at samsung if possible. If you found that irresistible, at andresson you will always be third if not fourth fiddle. . as it is part of the system there will be many failures, and you will be seen to be the fall guy. samsung will allow you to transition from one behemoth to another. do stuff you really are unique at doing. and has unlimited flexibility.
i never discuss with bill until negotiations are finished. lets talk about samsung later today

Met with them in sf yesterday.

From their perspective, giant offer. Basically peer with JK running their software adds to google android as well as their new phone operating system (so called tizen). Pretty much anything I want.

But something really big and substantial changes which was JK explicitly told me the new phone os was a backup plan meant to just take share from Microsoft and blackberry. We talked about this in great detail (he and I) in person.

Then in my offer, Tizen becomes the next big thing.

Since there is no way it can be there's an obvious game going on with JK. My guess is (after watching him work for years) that he 'lost' and sees me as a problem (stuff he used to manage and control now works for a white guy). So he changed tune to make his hedge seem really big so he can go off and do the phones the way he wants to.

Since I don't create a phone or make any products, just make software JK wants this is all really a bad spot.

I think they definitely want to hire me but just can't navigate their own org, Korea culture, and get over the importance of software.

Lots of money. Can work from anywhere but need to go to Korea a lot*. If they say one month at a time then they mean a lot more. All the people are so you have to. It would take 5 years to build a team here in us but even then I don't know what to build.

They will do most anything I want but I don't get to pick the most top level thing (work with google closely, sort of close, build Tizen).

I think they are in a precarious spot. Their NYC event rattled them too. Like I warned you.

Also talked to Andressen again. Seems appealing. I could do startup boards, learn the valley, and then be a full partner end of year. They need me. Goals are clear. Burden on me to do well which is good. Can work where I need to for a while (good for Melanie).

Apple just hired a guy from adobe. He's really good. Tim cook really needs help. Google needs help after firing their guy on android.

Existing Computer companies going through identity crises all at once. Finding something I can do for a while might be best path to take while I wait and see.

Did bill confide anything?
smasung feedback?
